parole.significato: alternative form of -я́к (-ják) (suffix usually denoting a person with a given characteristic, or an inanimate noun of…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -акъ (-akŭ), Proto-Slavic *-akъ.

parole.significato: The infinitive suffix for many verbs. Usually indicates an imperfective verb.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ati.

parole.significato: Used in place of -е́ть (-étʹ) after the hushing sibilants ш щ ч ж, when used to derive class-5 imperfective verbs from…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ati, from earlier *-ěti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *-ēˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₁- (stative suffix).

parole.significato: Suffix added to stems to show that it does something; a doer.
parole.testo: Combining form of де́ять (déjatʹ, “to do”), Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣꙗти (dějati), from Proto-Slavic *dějati, an extension of Proto-Slavic *děti (“to do, to say”) (whence деть (detʹ)), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dḗˀtei, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do”).

parole.significato: Suffix added to stems to show that it eats something; an eater.
parole.testo: From есть (jestʹ, “to eat”), Proto-Slavic *ěsti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ēˀstei, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti.

parole.significato: The infinitive suffix for some verbs; often indicates an intransitive or perfective verb. Becomes -ать (-atʹ) after hus…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ěti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *-ēˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₁- (stative suffix).

parole.significato: Suffix added to normally masculine nouns to form diminutives, sometimes with a further change in meaning.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ikъ.

parole.significato: the infinitive suffix for many verbs; usually indicates a perfective verb
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -ити (-iti), from Proto-Slavic *-iti.

parole.significato: forms nouns denoting the place where an occupation or office is performed
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьňa, from *-ьnъ + *-ja.

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns or sometimes other adjectives, often relational (meaning "related to X"): -ian, -ic,…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -ьскъ (-ĭskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ьskъ.

parole.significato: Reflexive suffix appended to finite verbs and infinitives to make a reflexive, reciprocal, intransitive or passive verb.
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic сѧ (sę), from Proto-Slavic *sę, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sen, from Proto-Indo-European *swé. It is considered the shortened form of себя́ (sebjá). Compare Belarusian and Ukrainian -ся (-sja), Italian -si, Spanish se.

parole.significato: but, and, while, although (deviates from the preceding idea in some manner; introduces a new or different meaning, as o…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic а (a, “and, but”), from Proto-Slavic *a (“and, but”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ōd (presumed to be the ablative of *éy, h₁e). Cognate with Lithuanian õ (“and, but”). Possible link with Lithuanian ar̃ (“question particle”). Compare Russian

parole.significato: to speak, to tell (also used in folklore or jocularly)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bàjati (“to tell”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bā́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéh₂ti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic бъдѣти (bŭděti, “to be awake”), from Proto-Slavic *bъděti (“to be awake”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *budḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běžati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bēˀgjā́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰégʷ-y-eh₂-ti, from *bʰegʷ- (“to flee, run”). 1-st person singular and 3-rd person plural, as well as imperative forms derive from бечь (bečʹ), from Proto-Slavic *běťi.

parole.significato: birchbark (bark of the birch tree, especially the paper birch)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic бересто (beresto), from Proto-Slavic *bersto.
Inherited from Old East Slavic береза (bereza), from Proto-Slavic *berza, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *berźas, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵós, whence English birch.
From Old East Slavic блъха (blŭxa), from Proto-Slavic *blъxa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *blúšāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlúseh₂.
From Old East Slavic блудъ (bludŭ), from Proto-Slavic *blǫdъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *blandás, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bordà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bardā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰéh₂. Doublet of брада́ (bradá) borrowed from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: borscht, borsht, borshch, borsch (a soup made of beets and cabbage)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъrščь, originally meaning “hogweed”, then “hogweed soup”, later “beetroot soup”, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bursktis.

Inherited from Old East Slavic бьрати (bĭrati), from Proto-Slavic *bьràti (“to take”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bírāˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti, whence English bear and Persian بردن (bordan, “to take, to carry”).

parole.significato: to clatter, to clang, to clank
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bręknǫti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *brínktei.

Inherited from Old East Slavic бꙑти (byti), from Proto-Slavic *byti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bū́ˀtei. Cognate with Ukrainian бути (buty), Belarusian быць (bycʹ), Polish być. Other cognates include Sanskrit भू (bhū, “to be”), Latin futūrus, and English be. The present forms are suppletive, from Prot
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *variti, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to burn”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьdova, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *widewāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂. Cognate with English widow, German Witwe, French veuve, Spanish viuda, Italian vedova, Sanskrit विधवा (vidhavā).

From Old East Slavic вѣньць (věnĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *věnьcь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *waiˀníkas, from Proto-Indo-European *woyh₁níkos. Cognate to вен (ven), венок (venok), ве́ник (vénik), вейка (vejka), вить (vitʹ).

parole.significato: all, the whole, all of, the whole of, the entire, the entirety of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсь (vĭsĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьśь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wišas. Cognate with Sanskrit विश्व (viśva, “all”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсь (vĭsĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьsь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wiśis, from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ-.

parole.significato: merry, cheerful, happy, convivial, gleeful, lighthearted
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *veselъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wéselas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wésus.

Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣтръ (větrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *větrъ. Cognates include English nirvana from Sanskrit निर्वाण (nirvāṇa, “blown or put out, extinguished”), and English weather, athlete, vent and wind.

PIE word  *wek(ʷ)speros From Old East Slavic вечеръ (večerŭ), from Proto-Slavic *večerъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wékeras, from Proto-Indo-European *wekʷsperos. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἕσπερος (hésperos) (whence Эспе́р (Espér), гесперо́рнис (gesperórnis), геспери́да (gesperída), геспери́дий (
Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣꙗти (vějati), from Proto-Slavic *vějati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁-.

Proto-Slavic *vъz-, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *uź-. Cognate with Lithuanian už (“within, instead of, in return for”), Latvian uz (“on, to”). Further etymology disputed. Compare also воз- (voz-), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Old East Slavic видъ (vidŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vidъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wéiˀdas, from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos, from *weyd-. Cognate with Lithuanian veidas (“face”), Latvian veids (“form, shape”), Sanskrit वेद (veda, “knowledge”), Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬉𐬛𐬀𐬵- (vaēdah-, “possession”), Lat

Inherited from Old East Slavic вода (voda), from Proto-Slavic *voda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wandō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥. Cognates include Sanskrit उद्र (udra), Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr) → English hydro-, English whisky and water.

parole.significato: to lead, to conduct, to guide
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *voditi (“to lead, conduct”). Cognate with English wed and wage.
Inherited from Old East Slavic вълкъ (vŭlkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьlkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wilkás, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьlna (“wool”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wílˀnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂ (“wool”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic вльна (vlĭna), Bulgarian въ́лна (vắlna), Serbo-Croatian ву̏на/vȕna, Czech vlna, Slovak vlna and Polish wełna.

Inherited from Old East Slavic володѣти (voloděti), from Proto-Slavic *volděti (“to rule”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *walˀdā́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁dʰh₁-, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule”). Doublet of владе́ть (vladétʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. Cognates include Ukrainian володі
Inherited from Old East Slavic волꙗ (volja), from Proto-Slavic *voľà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wáljāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic воронъ (voronŭ, “black”), from Proto-Slavic *vornъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *warnás. Related to Russian воро́на (voróna, “crow”), Lithuanian var̃nas (“crow, raven”). Doublet of вран (vran), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

From Old East Slavic ворона (vorona), from Proto-Slavic *vorna, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wárˀnāˀ. Related to Lithuanian várna (“crow”), Tocharian B wrauña (“crow”). Also related to Russian во́рон (vóron, “raven”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic воротити (vorotiti), from Proto-Slavic *vortiti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wártīˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *wortéyeti, from the root *wert-. Doublet of -врати́ть (-vratítʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic вратити (vratiti) (cf. возврати́ть (vozvratítʹ), изврат
PIE word  *oḱtṓw Inherited from Old East Slavic осмь (osmĭ), from Proto-Slavic *osmь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *aśtṓni, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.
Inherited from Old East Slavic осмъ (osmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *òsmъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *aśtmas.

From Old East Slavic выдра (vydra), from Proto-Slavic *vydra, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ūdrāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *udréh₂, the feminine form of *udrós, whence English otter and Sanskrit उद्र (udra). Doublet of ги́дра (gídra), which was borrowed from Greek.
From Old East Slavic глина (glina), from Proto-Slavic *glina, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gléiˀnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gleh₁y-.
From Old East Slavic гнѣздо (gnězdo), from Proto-Slavic *gnězdo, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nisdan, from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (whence also Latin nīdus, English nest).
Inherited from Old East Slavic говьно (govĭno), from Proto-Slavic *govьno, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gawāˀ, of uncertain origin.

From Old East Slavic годъ (godŭ, “time, period, year, age”), from Proto-Slavic *godъ (“suitable time”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gadás, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰodʰo-, from *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, be suitable”). Cognates include Ukrainian годі (hodi, “enough”), Bulgarian годе (gode, “e
Inherited from Old East Slavic голова (golova), from Proto-Slavic *golva, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *galˀwā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-. Doublet of глава́ (glavá) (Church Slavonicism).
From Old East Slavic голосъ (golosŭ), from Proto-Slavic *golsъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *galsás. Doublet of глас (glas), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic without pleophony.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gora, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *garā́ˀ.

parole.significato: to burn (to be consumed by fire)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gorěti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *garḗˀtei.
From Old East Slavic гость (gostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *gostь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gastís, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis. Cognate with English guest and host.
From Old East Slavic грѧда (gręda), from Proto-Slavic *grędà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *grindā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrendʰ-.
From Old East Slavic дань (danĭ), from Proto-Slavic *danь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀnis, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti (“to give”), whence English donate, date and data (via Latin and Romance). Also cognate with Sanskrit ददाति (dadāti), Sanskrit दान (dāna), Persian دادن and Latin dō.
Inherited from Old East Slavic дъва (dŭva), from Proto-Slavic *dъ̏va, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *duwō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic двьрь (dvĭrĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dvьrь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dwírs, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwṓr, whence English door, Lithuanian durys, Latin forum, Sanskrit द्वार (dvā́ra).
Inherited from Old East Slavic дъбрь (dŭbrĭ) : дьбрь (dĭbrĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dьbrь (“valley, ravine”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dubris, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰubr-, from *dʰewbʰ- (“deep”).
Old East Slavic девѧтъ (devętŭ), from Proto-Slavic *devę̃tъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dewintas.
Inherited from Old East Slavic девѧть (devętĭ), from Proto-Slavic *devętь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děliti (“to divide”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *doyl-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰayl-, *dʰoyl-. Cognates include Old English dǣlan (English deal) and Lithuanian dailyti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic десѧтъ (desętŭ), from Proto-Slavic *desętъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *deśimtás, from Proto-Indo-European *deḱm̥tós.

Inherited from Old East Slavic десѧть (desętĭ), from Proto-Slavic *desętь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *déśimt, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥t, whence English ten and deci-. Russian -дцать (-dcať) is from Proto-Indo-European *-dḱom̥t lately influenced by Proto-Slavic *desętь.

parole.significato: floor, bed (hard surface at the bottom of a body of water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic дъно (dŭno), from Proto-Slavic *dъno (“bottom”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dubnas, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰubnos, from *dʰewb- (“deep”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic добръ (dobrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ. Also related to Russian до́ба (dóba, “time”), Russian сдо́ба (sdóba, “shortening”), Russian удо́бный (udóbnyj, “comfortable”), Russian до́блесть (dóblestʹ, “valour”), Lithuanian dabà (“habit, character”), English daft, English d

From Old East Slavic долото (doloto), from Proto-Slavic *dolto, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dálbtan, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelbʰ-. Related to Russian долби́ть (dolbítʹ, “to peck, to gouge a hole in, to knock, to hit”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic долꙗ (dolja), from Proto-Slavic *doľa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dáljāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to divide”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic домъ (domŭ, “house; home”), from Proto-Slavic *dȍmъ (“house; home”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *damús, from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm (“home; house”)

Formed from дре́безг (drébezg, “jingle, tinkle”) + -а́ть (-átʹ, stative suffix). The root is from Proto-Slavic *drebězgъ, cognate with Lithuanian drebė̃znos pl, drebė̃nos pl (“remnants”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dreb-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drozdъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *trasdás, from Proto-Indo-European *trósdos.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drugъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *draugás, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ-.
From Old East Slavic дуга (duga), from Proto-Slavic *dǫga, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dangāˀ.

PIE word  *dʰuh₂mós Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-mós Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós Proto-Balto-Slavic *dū́ˀmas Proto-Slavic *dymъ Russian дым Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dymъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *degъtь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *degut(j)as, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ-. Cognate with Slovak decht. Likely a Baltic borrowing (cf. Lithuanian degùtas : dègti; Latvian deguts (“birch tar”) : degt). Absent in the South Slavic languages. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *že

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jebàti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *jebtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃yébʰeti, from *h₃yebʰ-. Cognate with Ancient Greek οἴφω (oíphō), Sanskrit यभति (yabhati). Compare Czech jebat, Polish jebać, Slovak jebať, Ukrainian їба́ти (jibáty), Serbo-Croatian јебати.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ěda, from *(j)ěsti (“to eat”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ḗˀstei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”). Cognates include Ancient Greek ἔδω (édō) (> ἔδεσμα (édesma)), Latin edō (> epulum, ēsca; see also prandium), Sanskrit अत्ति (átti), Lithuanian ė́sti (“to eat (of a
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ěsti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ēˀstei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic жѧдати (žędati), from Proto-Slavic *žę̄dàti (“to wish, desire”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gend-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰedʰ-.

parole.significato: to wait for (to stay where one is or delay action)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьdati (“to wait, to await”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *g(e)id-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeydʰ-. Compare Old High German gīt (“avarice”) and Old Prussian gēide (“they are waiting”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic же (že), from Proto-Slavic *že, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ge, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰi. Cognate with Czech že, Ancient Greek γε (ge), Sanskrit हि (hi), Ukrainian ж (ž).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьlna (“green woodpecker”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gilˀnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic зълчь (zŭlčĭ) (rarer жълчь (žŭlčĭ)), from Proto-Slavic *zьlčь (“bile”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źulʔ-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰlh₃-. Related to *zelenъ and was under the influence of *žьltъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic жена (žena), from Proto-Slavic *žena, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *génāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn, whence English queen and gyno-.

parole.significato: to burn (to cause something to be consumed by fire; to cause burns or a burning sensation in something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic жечи (žeči), from Proto-Slavic *žeťi (“to burn”) < *džetti < *džegti < *degti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *degtéi, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰégʷʰeti.

parole.significato: grain (any unground grain, such as rye, wheat, buckwheat, millet, barley, maize, oats)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žito (“grain, corn”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *géiˀtan, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃tom, from *gʷeyh₃-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žiti (compare Belarusian жыць (žycʹ), Ukrainian жи́ти (žýty), Old Church Slavonic жити (žiti)), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeih₃w- (“to live”). Cognate to Lithuanian gyventi, Sanskrit जीवति (jīvati, “lives”), Latin vīvō, and English quick.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьrьcь, from *žьrti + *-ьcь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *girˀ-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH-.
From Old East Slavic жьлтъ (žĭltŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žьltъ (“yellow”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gilˀtás, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”), whence English yellow.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *želǫdь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gel-, *gil-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьrny, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gírˀnūˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥h₂-n-uH-. Cognates include Sanskrit ग्रावन् (grāvan), Old Armenian երկան (erkan) and Old English cweorn (English quern).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *za.
From Old East Slavic звѣзда (zvězda), from Proto-Slavic *gvězda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źwaisdā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwoysdʰ-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic зима (zima), from Proto-Slavic *zima, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źeimā́ˀ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰéyōm.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źulas, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwel-.

parole.significato: to know: to be familiar with or accustomed to a person, place, or thing
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic знати (znati), from Proto-Slavic *znati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źnōˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéh₃t (“to know, get to know”), from *ǵneh₃-. Cognates include Polish znać, English know, kenning, canny, German kennen and Sanskrit ज्ञा (jñā, “to know”). For the col
Inherited from Old East Slavic зѫбъ (zǫbŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zǫbъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źámbas, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos. Cognate to Old Church Slavonic зѫбъ (zǫbŭ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic и́ва (íva), from Proto-Slavic *jь̀va, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *éiˀwāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHwéh₂ (“yew”). parole.significato: roe, spawn (of fish), also small eggs of frogs or other amphibia
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic икра (ikra), from Proto-Slavic *jьkrā, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ikrā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *yékʷr̥. Compare the semantic development of English roe; however, this is not an etymological cognate.

parole.significato: personal name, first name, Christian name, given name (for inanimate things, see назва́ние (nazvánije))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic имѧ (imę), from Proto-Slavic *jьmę, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *inˀmin, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥. Cognates include English name and noun, Old Prussian emmens, Sanskrit नामन् (nāman), Persian نام (nâm), Ancient Greek ὄνομα (ónoma), Latin nōmen. Neologism sense: ca
Inherited from Old East Slavic инъ (inŭ) from Proto-Slavic *jь̀nъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *iˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁inos.
Inherited from Old East Slavic какъ (kakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kakъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kōkos.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kaš(ь)ľь (“cough”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kaʔs(u)lio-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s- (whence also English whoost).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kašьľati (“to cough”), from *kaš(ь)ľь (“cough”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kāˀsulia, *kāˀslia, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s- (whence also English whoost).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kľučь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kljaukjas, from Proto-Indo-European *klewk-yo-s, from *kle(h₂)uk-, an extended form of *(s)kleh₂w- (“hook, key, peg”), whence English clef and close.
Inherited from Old East Slavic къи (kŷi), from Proto-Slavic *kъjь (“who, what, which”), from *kъ (“who”) + *-jь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kas (“who”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos (“who”).

parole.significato: to split, to cleave, to break (sugar), to crack (nuts), to chop (firewood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kòlti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic копати (kopati), from Proto-Slavic *kopati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kop-, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to strike, beat”).

parole.significato: to accumulate, to gather, to amass
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic копити (kopiti, “to amass, to gather, e.g. people for an army”), from Proto-Slavic *kopiti (“to stack, to pile, e.g. hay”), from *kopa (“heap, pile”), from *kopati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kop-, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to strike, beat”)

Inherited from Old East Slavic копие (kopije), from Proto-Slavic *kopьje (see details of derivation there), from *kopati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kop-, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to strike, beat”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic крꙑ (kry), from Proto-Slavic *kry, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *krū́ˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“blood of a wound”). Cognate with Latin cruor (“blood(shed)”), Lithuanian kraujas, Welsh crau, English raw.
From Old East Slavic кръха (krŭxa), from Proto-Slavic *krъxa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *krušā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *krows-.

parole.significato: to cover, to roof (a house); to thatch, to tile
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kryti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic лечи (leči), from Proto-Slavic *leťi, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *légtei, from Proto-Indo-European *légʰeti, from *legʰ-.

parole.significato: lime tree, linden (tree, wood, or flower)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic липа (lipa), from Proto-Slavic *lipa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *léiˀpāˀ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lomiti.
from Old East Slavic лукъ (lukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lǫkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lankás, from Proto-Indo-European *lenk- (“to bend”). Cognate with Lithuanian lankas.

Inherited from Old East Slavic лупити (lupiti, “to rob”), from Proto-Slavic *lupiti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *laupī́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“to peel, to break off”). Compare Albanian labë, German Laub, Latin liber.
Inherited from Old East Slavic лꙑко (lyko), from Proto-Slavic *lyko (“bast”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lúnˀkan (“bast”).
From Old East Slavic ледъ (ledŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ledъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ledús.
Inherited from Old East Slavic льнъ (lĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lьnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lína, from Proto-Indo-European *linom.

A nursery word. From Proto-Slavic *mama, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mā́ˀmāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-méh₂, a reduplication of *meh₂- - the root of *méh₂tēr (“mother”). Inherited from Old East Slavic мати (mati), from Proto-Slavic *mati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mā́ˀtē, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr, whence English mother and Sanskrit मातृ (mātṛ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic мьгла (mĭgla), from Proto-Slavic *mьgla, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *míglāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃migʰleh₂ (“mist, cloud”). Compare Polish mgła (“fog”).

parole.significato: abutment, abuttal, boundary, margin, division (as in land plots)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *meďa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *medjāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyeh₂. Ultimately from the feminine form of Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos. Cognate with English middle and mid, Latin medius, Sanskrit मध्य (mádhya) and Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *měsiti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *máiśīˀtei.

From Old East Slavic мѣхъ (měxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *měxъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *maišás, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *moysós. Cognates include Ukrainian міх (mix), Belarusian мех (mjex), Old Church Slavonic мѣхъ (měxŭ), Serbo-Croatian мијех/mijeh, Polish miech, Czech měch. Compare typolog

parole.significato: sack (large bag for storage and handling)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣшькъ (měšĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *měšьkъ, diminutive of *měxъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *maišás, from Proto-Indo-European *moysós. Compare typologically ко́жа (kóža) (<~ коза́ (kozá).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mirъ (“peace; world”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *meiˀrás (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey(H)-ró-s. parole.significato: to think, to imagine, to suspect
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьнѣти (mĭněti) or мьнити (mĭniti), from Proto-Slavic *mьněti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *minḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *men-. Cognate to Lithuanian miñti (“to recall, to mention”), Latvian minêt (“to mention”), Ancient Greek μέμονα (mémona, “to remember”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъnogъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *managas, from Proto-Indo-European *monogʰos.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mozgъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *masgás (“marrow; brain”), from Proto-Indo-European *mosgʰós. Cognate with Polish mózg, Serbo-Croatian мозак (mozak), Persian مغز (maġz), Dutch merg, English marrow.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мои (moi), from Proto-Slavic *mojь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *majas, from Proto-Indo-European *móyos (“my; mine”). Cognate with Old Prussian mais.

parole.significato: to implore, to entreat, to beseech
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic молити (moliti), from Proto-Slavic *modlìti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *maldī́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *meldʰ-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic мълниꙗ (mŭlnija), мълнии (mŭlnii), from Proto-Slavic *mъlnьji or *mьlnьji, from earlier *mъldnьji or *mъldni, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mild-n-, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dʰ-n- (“lightning”). parole.significato: to grind, to mill (to make smaller by breaking with a device)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *melti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mélˀtei.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мостъ (mostŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mostъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mastás.
Inherited from Old East Slavic моча (moča), from Proto-Slavic *moča / *močь (“wetness, puddle, urine”), from *mok- + *-ja, *-jь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mok-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic мудръ (mudrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mǫdrъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mandras, from Proto-Indo-European *mondʰh₁ros, from *men(s)dʰh₁- + *-rós. Cognate with Lithuanian mandrùs and Proto-Germanic *mundraz (German munter).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *murava, from *mura, *murъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mauˀras (“mud”). Cognate with Polish murawa.
From Old East Slavic мꙑшь (myšĭ), from Proto-Slavic *myšь (“mouse”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mū́ˀšis, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs. The computing term is a semantic loan from English mouse.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мѧкъкъ (mękŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *minˀkakas, from Proto-Indo-European *mn̥k-o-kó-s, from *menk-.

From Old East Slavic нить (nitĭ), from Proto-Slavic *nitь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nī́ˀtis, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁-.

From Old East Slavic небо (nebo), from Proto-Slavic *nebo, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nébas, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos. Doublet of не́бо (nébo), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ovьnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *awinas.

Inherited from Old East Slavic огнь (ognĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ogňь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ugnis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnis. Inherited from Old East Slavic озеро (ozero), from Proto-Slavic *ȅzero, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *éźeran.

From Old East Slavic орьлъ (orĭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orьlъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *arélis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃érō.

Inherited from Old East Slavic пьрвъ (pĭrvŭ, “first”), from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pírˀwas, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥h₂wós, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“before, formerly; through, throughout”). Baltic cognates include Lithuanian pi̇̀rmas (“first; primary”),
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pěstъ.

From Old East Slavic печи (peči), from Proto-Slavic *peťi, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *péktei, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷeti, from *pekʷ-. Inherited from Old East Slavic пизда́ (pizdá), from Proto-Slavic *pīzdà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pīˀsdāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *písdeh₂.

parole.significato: to push, to shove, to elbow
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic пьхати (pĭxati), from Proto-Slavic *pьxati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pištei, from Proto-Indo-European *pis-é-ti, from *peys- (“to crush”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic плесна (plesna), from Proto-Slavic *pľusna, an alternative form of *plesno, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pl(j)ousk-. Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pílˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós. Cognates include Latin plenus → English replenish, Sanskrit पूर्ण (pūrṇa) and English full.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьlxъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *letъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lekt-, from Proto-Indo-European *lek- (“jump”).

parole.significato: to remember, to recollect, to think of, to keep in mind
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic помьнити (pomĭniti), from Proto-Slavic *pomьněti or *pomьniti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *minḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *mn-eh₁- (present stem *mn-eye-), from the root *men- (“to think, mind”). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic помьнѣти (pomĭněti), Polish pomnieć

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pravъ. Compare пра́вда (právda). Cognate with Latin prōvincia (“territory, dominion, office, duty, province”), Proto-Germanic *frawjô (“lord”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic прѣснъ (prěsnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *prěsnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *prḗˀskas. Cognate with English fresh.

parole.significato: with; when; during (in the time and/or presence (of))
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pri, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *prei, from Proto-Indo-European *préy, whence English for and per.
Inherited from Old East Slavic про (pro), from Proto-Slavic *pro, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pra, from Proto-Indo-European *pró.

parole.significato: through, past (describing an action of passing through a space or an object)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic про- (pro-), from Proto-Slavic *pro-.

From Old East Slavic просити (prositi), from Proto-Slavic *prositi, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *práśīˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ-. Distantly related to English pray and precarious. Indo-European cognates include Persian پرسیدن (porsidan), Northern Kurdish pirsîn, Sanskrit पृच्छति (pṛccháti), A
From Old East Slavic путь (putĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pǫtь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pántis, from Proto-Indo-European *póntoh₁s (whence also Latin pōns, Ancient Greek πόντος (póntos), English find).
Inherited from Old East Slavic пьшено (pĭšeno), from Proto-Slavic *pьšeno, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pišenan, from Proto-Indo-European *pis-e-no-m, from *peys-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pęstь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic пѧтъ (pętŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pętъ, from Proto-Slavic *pętъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *penktas, from Proto-Indo-European *penkʷtós..
From Old East Slavic ребро (rebro), from Proto-Slavic *rebrò, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rébran, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ-.

parole.significato: to cut up, to cut open, to slice, to carve
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic рѣзати (rězati), from Proto-Slavic *rězati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rḗˀźtei, from Proto-Indo-European *wreh₁ǵ-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic рѣзати (rězati), Ukrainian різати (rizaty), Bulgarian режа (reža), Serbo-Croatian резати, Slovene rezati, Czech řezat, Slovak rezať,
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rogъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rágas. The irregular plural рога́ (rogá) is an old dual form.

parole.significato: generation, birth, origin, stock, family, race, tribe, lineage
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic родъ (rodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rodъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *radás. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”), whence English root. Cognates include Latvian rads, Ukrainian рід (rid) and Polish ród amongst others.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rozga, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *razgā́ˀ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)resg-. Cognates include Latin restis, Old Armenian երագազ (eragaz). Compare typologically плеть (pletʹ) akin to плести́ (plestí).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rosà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rasā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rṓs.
From Old East Slavic рѫка (rǫka), from Proto-Slavic *rǫka, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ránkāˀ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic самъ (samŭ), from Proto-Slavic *samъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sāmas, from Proto-Indo-European *somHós.

Inherited from Old East Slavic свинꙑ́и (svinýi), from Proto-Slavic *svinъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *swīˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *suH-iHnos, from *suH- (“pig, hog, swine”) + *-iHnos. By surface analysis, сви(нья́) (svi(nʹjá)) + -но́й (-nój).

Inherited from Old East Slavic сь (sĭ, “this”), from Proto-Slavic *sь (“this”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *śis, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱís. Doublet of сий (sij), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. Also compare to Ukrainian цей (cej).
From Old East Slavic сѣмѧ (sěmę), from Proto-Slavic *sěmę, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sḗˀmin, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥, whence English seed and semen.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sěno, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *śáina. Compare to Lithuanian šienas.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сестра (sestra), from Proto-Slavic *sestra, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
From Old East Slavic сѣсти (sěsti), from Proto-Slavic *sěsti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sḗˀstei, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣꙗти (sějati), from Proto-Slavic *sějati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁-ye-ti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣдѣти (sěděti), from Proto-Slavic *sěděti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sēdḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sila, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *séiˀlāˀ. Cognates include Lithuanian si̇́ela.
Inherited from Old East Slavic слава (slava), from Proto-Slavic *slàva.
From Old East Slavic слѣдъ (slědŭ), from Proto-Slavic *slědъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sláidus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sleydʰ-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic смьрдѣти (smĭrděti), from Proto-Slavic *smьrdě̀ti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *smirˀdḗˀtei.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sněgъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *snáigas, from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos.

parole.significato: to move to and fro, to scurry about, to whisk, to dash about, to skirr, to fuss
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *snovati.
From Old East Slavic сокъ (sokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sȍkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sakás, from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷós.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *soldъkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *salˀdus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂l-. Doublet of сла́дкий (sládkij).

From Old East Slavic спѣти (spěti), from Proto-Slavic *spěti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *spḗˀtei from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁-, whence English spare. Akin to Slovene speti, Slovak dospieť, Czech spět. Non-Slavic cognates include Ossetian ӕфсад (æfsad) and Latin spes.
Inherited from Old East Slavic стьзꙗ (stĭzja), from Proto-Slavic *stьdza (“path”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *stigaˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *stigʰ-eh₂.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сторожь (storožĭ), from Proto-Slavic *storžь (“guard”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *storʔg-. Doublet of страж (straž), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: terrible, scary [with instrumental or в (v, + prepositional) ‘in (e.g. one's rage)’] (literally or as an intensifier)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *strašьnъ, from *straxъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *strākš-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)treg-. By surface analysis, страх (strax) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *strъjь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сѫдъ (sǫdŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сꙑнъ (synŭ), from Proto-Slavic *synъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sū́ˀnus, from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús.  PIE word  *suHnús
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *syrъ (“cheese”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sū́ˀras, from Proto-Indo-European *súHros.
From Old East Slavic твьрдъ (tvĭrdŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tvьrdъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *twírˀtas, from Proto-Indo-European *twerH-. Doublet of кварц (kvarc).

Inherited from Old East Slavic тътъ (tŭtŭ), reduplication of Proto-Slavic *tъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tas, from Proto-Indo-European *só, *séh₂, *tód (“this, that”). Cognate with Old Polish tet, Latvian tas, Lithuanian tas, ta, Sanskrit स (sá), Sanskrit तत् (tat), Old English se (whence English the

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъščь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tuskjas, from Proto-Indo-European *tus-sḱ-yós, from *tews- (“to empty”), from *tew- (“to swell”). Cognate with Polish czczy, Lithuanian tùščias, Latvian tukšs, Vedic Sanskrit तुच्छ्य (tucchyá), Persian تهی (tohi).
Inherited from Old East Slavic треть (tretĭ), from Proto-Slavic *tretь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tretias.
Inherited from Old East Slavic трие (trije), from Proto-Slavic *trьje, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tríjes, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tỳsęťa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tū́ˀsantis, from Proto-Indo-European *tuHsont-. Cognate with Ukrainian тисяча (tysjača), Serbo-Croatian тисућа, tisuća, Slovene tisoč, Czech and Slovak tisíc, Polish tysiąc. Akin to English thousand, Gothic 𐌸𐌿𐍃𐌿𐌽𐌳𐌹 (þūsundi), Lithuanian t
Inherited from Old East Slavic тьма (tĭma), from Proto-Slavic *tьma, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *timāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *temH-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тѧжькъ (tęžĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tęžьkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tingús, from Proto-Indo-European *tengʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *u-

parole.significato: coal (a black rock formed from prehistoric plant remains, composed largely of carbon and burned as a fuel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic угъль (ugŭlĭ) or угль (uglĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫglь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ánˀglis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óngʷl̥ (“charcoal”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic ѫгль (ǫglĭ).

parole.significato: good luck, success (achievement of one's aim or goal)
parole.testo: Derived from уда́ться (udátʹsja), and then у- (u-) + дать (datʹ). Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti (“to give”), whence English donate, date and data.

Inherited from Old East Slavic усъ (usŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫsъ < *vǫsъ < *vǫdsъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wónsa, from Proto-Indo-European *wondʰsom, s-expansion of root *wendʰ- (“hair, wool, beard”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic уха (uxa), from Proto-Slavic *juxa, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yew(ǝ)- (“to blend, mix (food), knead”). Cognates include Latin ius (whence English juice), Ancient Greek ζύμη (zúmē) (whence Russian энзи́м (enzím, “enzyme, ferment”)), Proto-Germanic *justaz, Sa

parole.significato: to teach, to instruct (often not in an academic setting)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic учити (učiti), from Proto-Slavic *učiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic цвѣтъ (cvětŭ). Cognate with English white. Doublet of свет (svet).
From Old East Slavic цѣлъ (cělŭ), from Proto-Slavic *cělъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *káilas. Compare Czech celý.

From Old East Slavic цѣна (cěna), from Proto-Slavic *cěna, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kainā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂, from *kʷey- (“to pay”), whence English pain and penalty. Probably, a doublet of пе́ня (pénja, “fine”).

parole.significato: bewitchment, witchcraft, magic, incantation, sorcery, spell
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čarъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ker-, *kēr-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic чьи (čĭi), from Proto-Slavic *čьjь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kijas.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *česàti (“to comb, to scratch”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *késtei. Per Vasmer, cognates include Sanskrit कच्छू (kacchū, “an itch, a scab”), Ancient Greek κεσκέον (keskéon, “oakum, tow”) and Ancient Greek κέωρος (kéōros, “nettle”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic четвьртъ (četvĭrtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtъ (“fourth”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ketwirtas, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥tós.

PIE word  *kʷetwóres Inherited from Old East Slavic четꙑре (četyre), from Proto-Slavic *četỳre, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ketū́res, Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Cognates include Proto-Iranian *čaθwā́rah, Sanskrit चत्वार (catvā́ra-, m.pl.).
Inherited from Old East Slavic шестъ (šestŭ), from Proto-Slavic *šȅstъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *seśtas, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱstós.
Inherited from Old East Slavic шесть (šestĭ), from Proto-Slavic *šestь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *šéš, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šiti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sjū́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *syewH-. Cognate to Lithuanian siūti, English sew, Latin suō.

Inherited from Old East Slavic щитъ (ščitŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ščitъ (“shield”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *skeita, from Proto-Indo-European *skey-to-m, from *skey- (“to cut, separate”). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian štit, Old Irish scíath, Latin scūtum.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗгода (jagoda), from Proto-Slavic *agoda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ṓˀgāˀ.
From Old East Slavic ꙗзва (jazva), from Proto-Slavic *jazva, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *áiˀźwāˀ. Cognate to Old Prussian eyswo (“wound”), Lithuanian áiža, Latvian aĩza.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ѧзꙑкъ (językŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ęzykъ, from Early Proto-Slavic *inzū́kus, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *inźūˀs, from earlier *dinźūˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s, whence English tongue and Latin lingua, whence language.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗице (jaice), from Proto-Slavic *ājьcè, diminutive of *ȃje (“egg”), ultimately from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ṓjan (“egg”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (“egg”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗсли (jasli), from Proto-Slavic *jasli, from earlier Proto-Slavic *ědsli-, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ēd-. Related to Russian есть (jestʹ, “to eat”), Russian еда́ (jedá, “food”), Russian я́ство (jástvo), Russian я́стель (jástelʹ, “eater”).
